notes: \cpara{Recalls the previous day's case and its conclusion: she defended ``I believe'' while seeming not to believe.}
\cpara{Introduces the Litany of Tarski, the author's formula from ``The Meditation on Curiosity'' (2007): desire to believe a thing if and only if it is so.}
\cpara{The litany, in its sky example.}
\cpara{The question: if it were known that God does not exist, should she still believe in God?}
\cpara{The author's first reading of her hesitation: attachment to a world with God in it.}

\cpara{The revised reading, hedged (``I suspect''): her thoughts were all about her belief, and God was not a node in her model of the world. It is an inference from one hesitation over one question.}
\cpara{Announces her ``counterexample'' to the litany.}
\cpara{Her sentence has the form that philosophers discuss as Moore's paradox: ``I believe that p, but not p.'' The author names the paradox three days later, in ``Moore's Paradox.''}

\cpara{Explains to her that saying something expresses belief in it, so ``I believe people are nice'' expresses a belief about her belief. That assertion expresses belief is one standard starting point for explaining why sentences like hers are odd (Wikipedia, ``Moore's paradox'').}

\cpara{The line is from Wittgenstein's \textsc{Philosophical Investigations}, Part II, section x, a section that discusses ``I believe'' and states Moore's paradox. The post's wording matches the translation, apart from one comma. In the same passage Wittgenstein says that ``the expression `I believe that this is the case' is used like the assertion `This is the case'.'' That is not the reading the author gave her a paragraph earlier, that saying ``I believe people are nice'' means you believe you believe it.}

\cpara{Her reply keeps the sentence and adds that she put it that way ``for you.'' The post does not say what she meant by that, though the wording it goes on to analyse was, by her own account, chosen for her listener.}
\cpara{Quotes Nanny Ogg in Terry Pratchett's \textsc{Maskerade} on a mind ``all tangled up like a ball of string.'' I could not check the wording against the novel.}
\cpara{Says the author can name her failure (her reasoning is not ``consistent under reflection'') but still cannot grasp it.}
\cpara{Says the author can imagine the minds of characters in the author's own fiction but not hers, and asks whether that is unwillingness.}

\cpara{A general claim about intelligent religious people, that they have only a limited time to become atheists. ``This is why'' presents it as following from her case. It rests on one conversation and nothing else.}
\cpara{An aside: she said it is good to believe that someone cares whether you do right or wrong.}
\cpara{The author's reply, that a human caring should be enough, stopped her ``for a bit.''}
\cpara{She answers that nothing should be done differently if there were definitely no God.}
\cpara{The author's reply, with a joke about how a rabbi would take her answer.}

\cpara{Concludes, hedged (``seems''), that her religion is the worship of worship. The next sentence drops the hedge: she ``now believes that belief in God will save her.'' She is not reported as saying anything about being saved.}
\cpara{Reports the question whether she is always surprised when people fall short of her expectations, and her long pause.}
\cpara{Explains what the question was meant to show: that believing falsely would bring constant disappointment.}
\cpara{A claim about the whole of her philosophy is drawn from a pause, and stated as a realization (``I now realize''), without a hedge.}

\cpara{Concludes that she worships her own attempt at self-deception, and that ``The attempt failed, but she is honestly unaware of this.'' The previous day's ``so far as I can tell'' is gone; the evidence is the same conversation.}
\cpara{Draws a program from the case: those defending sanity must now oppose the worship of the supposed benefits of faith.}
\cpara{Refers to ``Doublethink'' (2007), which said: ``You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will.''}
\cpara{Restates that claim (``you can't just choose to believe the sky is green'') and adds the new point: if you do not realize it, you can believe you have deceived yourself.}
\cpara{The placebo claim, offered the day before with ``I suppose,'' is stated here without a hedge. No evidence is added.}

\cpara{Describes the author's arguments that self-deception is hard as aimed at an effect: removing the placebo benefit. Four days later the author says more about this (see the notes on ``Don't Believe You'll Self-Deceive'').}
\cpara{Asks whether theists will next defend belief in belief, or belief in belief in belief.}

\cpara{An aside against the zombie argument in the philosophy of mind, said to have ``gotten even more tangled than this.'' The argument is not stated; the link is to the author's ``Zombies! Zombies?'' (2008).}
\cpara{Invites commenters to defend belief in belief in belief.}
